rule_name: Subordinate Instead of Chaining With "And" / "Then"
quote: started it last year and Mrs. Aldana has been adding to it since September, and Chloe doesn't know about either of those things
why: three clauses are coordinated with "and" and given equal grammatical weight instead of being subordinated into a hierarchy
suggestion: After her kindergarten teacher started it last year, Mrs. Aldana has kept adding to it since September, without Chloe knowing either thing.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a while
why: "for a while" is used here as a generic duration marker regardless of what kind of moment is being timed
suggestion: She listens through two more sentences, and Chloe hears her switch the phone to her other ear.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: Chloe hears her switch the phone to her other ear.
why: this is the rule's own banned example verbatim, routing the sound through the perception verb instead of rendering it directly
suggestion: The phone clicks as her mom switches it to her other ear.

rule_name: Negative Framing and Minimisation, State What a Thing Is
quote: She is not really listening to the phone call, but she is not turning any pages either.
why: defines Chloe's state through two denials instead of committing to what she is actually doing
suggestion: She sits on the living room floor with the book open, staring at the same page.

rule_name: Subordinate Instead of Chaining With "And" / "Then"
quote: Chloe does the first one, and then the second one, which is 8 − 3, and partway through the second one she gets how it works.
why: this is nearly identical to the rule's own banned example, chaining clauses with "and" instead of subordinating them
suggestion: After the first one, she does the second, which is 8 minus 3, and partway through it, she sees how it works.

rule_name: Dialogue Formatting and Typography
why: breaks the chapter's otherwise consistent spelled-out numeral convention (thirty, twenty-eight, eleven) with digits
suggestion: eight minus three

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: there is nothing left in the worksheet to find out
why: verbatim reuse of the rule's own banned vague-abstraction example
suggestion: she has already found the pattern, and the rest is only copying it twenty-seven more times

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: is nothing at all
why: "nothing at all" is a gray placeholder standing in for what actually happens during those eleven minutes
suggestion: so the next eleven minutes is Bryce still counting on his fingers

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: which she has done twice already this morning
why: near-verbatim match to the rule's own banned crutch phrase "which she has done X times already"
suggestion: her thumb finds the corner of it without looking, the way it already has twice since the bell

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Interiority of non-POV characters)
quote: where he thinks Mrs. Aldana can't see him
why: attributes an unearned belief to Bryce, a non-POV character, which the style guide bans in narration
suggestion: under the edge of his desk, out of Mrs. Aldana's sightline

rule_name: Keep Narrative Tense Consistent Unless the Break Is Signalled
quote: She didn't know there had been one, because she was in the parking lot.
why: drops into simple past ("didn't," "was") with no signal, inside an otherwise present-tense narrative
suggestion: She doesn't know there has been one, because she is in the parking lot.

rule_name: Negative Framing and Minimisation, State What a Thing Is
quote: Mrs. Aldana doesn't say it mean. She says it tired.
why: denies a reading ("mean") that nobody in the scene has asserted before stating the positive fact
suggestion: Mrs. Aldana says it tired.

rule_name: Adjective-as-Adverb Dialogue Tags ("She Says It Tired")
quote: She says it tired.
why: verbatim match to the rule's own banned adjective-as-adverb dialogue tag
suggestion: she says, not looking up from the worksheet

rule_name: Dialogue That States the Theme, Cut the Character's Gloss on Their Own Image
quote: Which is the whole thing. That's the whole book, right there, in the bowl.
why: Chloe explains the meaning of the locker-key image immediately after rendering it, replacing the reader's own arrival at the point
suggestion: cut these two sentences and let the image close the beat: "...and nobody put it there on purpose, it just ended up there."

rule_name: Match Syntax to the Age, With the Ability Built In
quote: Because at the start the key is the most important thing either of them has, and at the end it's just in with the batteries and the rubber bands, and nobody put it there on purpose, it just ended up there. And that's how you know they're okay.
why: a six-year-old delivering fully worked literary symbolism with this much subordination reads as an adult's thesis rather than age-appropriate grammar carrying precocious content
suggestion: At the start the key is the biggest thing they have. At the end it's just in the bowl with the batteries. Nobody put it there. That's how you know.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: The whole thing takes forty minutes.
why: repeats the chapter's overused "the whole thing" crutch, listed by name as a banned phrase
suggestion: Bedtime takes forty minutes.

rule_name: 5. The trailing clause
quote: which it is
why: the sentence is complete and correct before the comma; the trailing clause only tells the reader how to take "funny" instead of adding a fact
suggestion: Her mom tells somebody about it on the phone later, like it's funny.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: the part where
why: verbatim match to the rule's banned placeholder phrase "the part where," standing in for behavior that should be shown
suggestion: Chloe hears her mother tell someone she had to be told three times to eat.

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: Chloe hears the part where her mom says she had to be told three times to eat
why: routes the overheard remark through the filter verb "hears" instead of rendering the words directly
suggestion: "She had to be told three times to eat," her mom says into the phone, laughing.

rule_name: The Said-Bookism Overcorrection, Vary Attribution in Long Exchanges
quote: Maddie was out. She caught it on one bounce and she was out, and that was like four minutes ago, so either one bounce is out or it isn't.
why: opens three consecutive untagged turns in a longer exchange, sparser than the rule's own cited failure of one tag across four turns
suggestion: "Maddie was out," Chloe says, still facing the fence. "She caught it on one bounce and she was out..."

rule_name: Use Past Perfect for Action Before the Narrative Present
quote: Chloe read a book about Icarus at the library two weeks ago and thought about it for four days afterward.
why: verbatim reuse of the rule's own example, using simple past for action before the narrative present instead of past perfect
suggestion: Chloe had read a book about Icarus at the library two weeks ago and had thought about it for four days afterward.

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction, Don't Normalise by Reporting an Absent Reaction
quote: Nobody says anything, though a chair squeaks somewhere behind her.
why: reports an absent collective reaction as evidence the moment passed unremarked, the construction the rule bans
suggestion: A chair squeaks somewhere behind her. Peanut keeps washing his face.

rule_name: Negative Framing and Minimisation, State What a Thing Is
quote: She isn't being mean about it.
why: defines Kayleigh's tone by what it is not instead of stating plainly what it is
suggestion: Kayleigh says it like a fact, not an insult.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for her that's the end of it
why: near-verbatim match to the rule's banned reflexive scene-closer "and that's the end of it"
suggestion: cut it and let the action close the beat: "She says it, turns back around."

rule_name: Telling After Showing, Don't Explain the Image You Just Rendered
quote: She doesn't cry.
why: narrates the restraint that the flat "Yeah" already showed, explaining an image that already did the work
suggestion: cut the sentence; let "Yeah," Chloe says stand on its own before the next beat

rule_name: Keep Narrative Tense Consistent Unless the Break Is Signalled
quote: It was either the Icarus or the saying it a second time louder
why: drops into simple past with no signal inside otherwise present-tense narration
suggestion: It's either the Icarus or the saying it a second time louder

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction, Don't Normalise by Reporting an Absent Reaction
quote: Nobody turns around.
why: verbatim match to the rule's own banned example of the "Nobody" construction
suggestion: Mrs. Aldana moves on to the next thing on the board, and Chloe puts her hand back down.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: The whole thing takes about two seconds
why: repeats the chapter's overused "the whole thing" placeholder a third time
suggestion: The exchange takes about two seconds

rule_name: Banned Constructions, Assert Nothing, Show the Substance
quote: which is correct and is one word
why: "which is correct" is a close variant of the banned verdict phrase "that is correct," asserting rightness instead of showing it
suggestion: and she says clouds, one word, again

rule_name: 8. Automatic-fail narrator constructions (Superlatives in narration)
quote: Everybody is always right.
why: an absolute superlative delivered by the narrator, a construction the style guide says is fine in dialogue but fails in narration
suggestion: So far this year, every guess has landed.

rule_name: The "Nobody" Construction, Don't Normalise by Reporting an Absent Reaction
quote: nobody says anything at all
why: another instance of the banned construction, reporting an absent reaction as evidence of the room's response
suggestion: Maddie looks down at her own desk.

rule_name: Thought Reported vs. Thought Rendered
quote: Chloe thinks about the parking lot, and the boxes, and not knowing there had been a question.
why: states that Chloe thought about these things rather than rendering the thought itself happening
suggestion: The parking lot. The boxes. The question that had already happened without her.

rule_name: Thought Reported vs. Thought Rendered
quote: Chloe thinks about that one for a while.
why: near-verbatim match to the rule's own banned example of reported rather than rendered thought
suggestion: Almost all of the time, she knows. Except—

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a while
why: generic duration crutch reused again as a universal timer
suggestion: Chloe turns that one over through two more of his questions.

rule_name: Crutch Phrases That Have Stopped Meaning Anything
quote: for a while
why: the same generic duration crutch reused a third time in the chapter
suggestion: types for three lines without saying anything

rule_name: Filtering, Cut "She Sees / Hears / Notices / Knows"
quote: which is how she hears her dad say she was quiet tonight
why: routes the overheard remark through the filter verb "hears" instead of rendering it directly
suggestion: "She was quiet tonight," her dad says, and she is awake enough to hear it.

rule_name: Use Past Perfect for Action Before the Narrative Present
quote: Chloe read the whole thing on Tuesday. She read the ending sitting on the bathroom floor at home, because she couldn't wait until after dinner to find out whether the dog lived.
why: simple past used for action before the narrative present instead of past perfect, echoing the same slip as line 50
suggestion: Chloe had read the whole thing on Tuesday. She had read the ending sitting on the bathroom floor at home, because she couldn't have waited until after dinner to find out whether the dog lived.

rule_name: Keep Narrative Tense Consistent Unless the Break Is Signalled
quote: She got in trouble for reading, in reading.
why: drops into simple past for the closing line of an otherwise present-tense paragraph, with no signaled break
suggestion: She gets in trouble for reading, in reading.

rule_name: Ration a Character's Verbal Tic to the Moments It Characterises
quote: The whole dinner takes nine minutes.
why: verbatim match to the rule's own cited example of the narrator's counting tic becoming a reflexive default rather than a signal
suggestion: Her mom is at the sink before anyone else is finished eating.

rule_name: Vague Abstractions, Replace "Something," "Nothing," "The Whole Thing"
quote: Then something goes out of her mom's face. Chloe watches it go without knowing what it's for.
why: "something" and "it" stand in for a specific, nameable expression instead of naming it
suggestion: Then the corner of her mom's mouth drops and doesn't come back up before she turns to the sink.

rule_name: Negative Framing and Minimisation, State What a Thing Is
quote: So the boring part isn't the problem, because the other kids sit through it fine.
why: defines "the problem" by what it is not instead of stating directly what it is
suggestion: The other kids sit through it fine; Chloe is the one who can't.
